subject: Biology
title: Carnivorous Plants
description: Learn Carnivorous Plants in one minute.

hook.text: In nutrient-poor bogs, some plants gave up waiting for minerals in soil—and started eating animals.

buildup.text: Venus flytraps snap shut in 100 milliseconds when trigger hairs are touched twice.

discovery.text: Sundews use sticky tentacles. Pitcher plants drown insects in pools of digestive enzymes.

twist.text: Carnivorous plants still photosynthesize. They eat insects for nitrogen and phosphorus, not energy.

climax.text: Over 600 species of carnivorous plants evolved independently across different continents.

punchline.text: When the soil can't feed you, eat the visitors.

quiz.question: Why do carnivorous plants eat insects?
options: To get nitrogen and phosphorus from poor soil

details.summary: Carnivorous plants capture and digest insects and other small animals to obtain nitrogen and phosphorus scarce in their boggy, acidic habitats. Venus flytraps use snap traps, sundews use sticky tentacles, and pitcher plants drown prey in enzyme-filled pools.
details.whyItMatters: Carnivorous plants demonstrate that evolution finds creative solutions to nutrient scarcity. They challenge the assumption that plants are passive organisms and reveal the incredible diversity of survival strategies in the plant kingdom.
takeaways: Venus flytraps snap shut in under a second when trigger hairs are touched twice
Pitcher plants trap insects in slippery modified leaves filled with digestive fluids
Carnivory evolved independently at least six times in different plant lineages

faq.question: Why did some plants evolve to eat insects?
faq.answer: Carnivorous plants typically grow in nutrient-poor soils where nitrogen and phosphorus are scarce. Capturing insects provides these essential nutrients. The evolutionary cost of building traps is offset by the nutritional benefit in environments where roots alone cannot supply enough.

faq.question: How does a Venus flytrap know when to snap shut?
faq.answer: Each trap has three to four trigger hairs on its inner surface. Two touches within 20 seconds are needed to spring the trap, preventing false triggers from rain or debris. The snap uses a rapid change in cell turgor pressure that inverts the leaf lobes in under a second.
